In [[mathematics]], specifically in the field of [[topology]], a [[topological space]] is said to be a '''door space''' if every subset is [[Open set|open]] or [[Closed set|closed]] (or [[Clopen set|both]]).{{sfn|Kelley|1975|loc=ch.2, Exercise C, p. 76}}  The term comes from the introductory topology mnemonic that "a subset is not like a door: it can be open, closed, both, or neither".

==Properties and examples==

Every door space is [[T0-space|T<sub>0</sub>]] (because if <math>x</math> and <math>y</math> are two [[topologically indistinguishable]] points, the singleton <math>\{x\}</math> is neither open nor closed).

Every [[subspace (topology)|subspace]] of a door space is a door space.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Dontchev |first1=Julian |title=On door spaces |journal=Indian Journal of Pure and Applied Mathematics |date=1995 |volume=26 |issue=9 |pages=873–881 |url=https://www.insa.nic.in/writereaddata/UpLoadedFiles/IJPAM/20005a1b_873.pdf }} Theorem 2.6</ref>  So is every [[quotient (topology)|quotient]] of a door space.{{sfn|Dontchev|1995|loc=Corollary 2.12}}

Every topology [[finer topology|finer than]] a door topology on a set <math>X</math> is also a door topology.

Every [[discrete space]] is a door space.  These are the spaces without [[accumulation point]], that is, whose every point is an [[isolated point]].

Every space <math>X</math> with exactly one accumulation point (and all the other point isolated) is a door space (since subsets consisting only of isolated points are open, and subsets containing the accumulation point are closed).  Some examples are: (1) the [[one-point compactification]] of a discrete space (also called [[Fort space]]), where the point at infinity is the accumulation point; (2) a space with the [[excluded point topology]], where the "excluded point" is the accumulation point.

Every [[Hausdorff space|Hausdorff]] door space is either discrete or has exactly one accumulation point. (To see this, if <math>X</math> is a space with distinct accumulation points <math>x</math> and <math>y</math> having respective disjoint [[neighbourhood]]s <math>U</math> and <math>V,</math> the set <math>(U\setminus\{x\})\cup\{y\}</math> is neither closed nor open in <math>X.</math>)<ref>{{cite web |title=Proving that If $(X,\tau)$ is a Hausdorff door space, then at most one point $x \in X$ is a limit point of $X$ |url=https://math.stackexchange.com/questions/3789612 |website=Mathematics Stack Exchange}}</ref>

An example of door space with more than one accumulation point is given by the [[particular point topology]] on a set <math>X</math> with at least three points.  The open sets are the subsets containing a particular point <math>p\in X,</math> together with the empty set.  The point <math>p</math> is an isolated point and all the other points are accumulation points. (This is a door space since every set containing <math>p</math> is open and every set not containing <math>p</math> is closed.)  Another example would be the [[topological sum]] of a space with the particular point topology and a discrete space.

Door spaces <math>(X,\tau)</math> with no isolated point are exactly those with a topology of the form <math>\tau=\mathcal U \cup \{\emptyset\}</math> for some [[free ultrafilter]] <math>\mathcal U</math> on <math>X.</math><ref>{{cite journal |last1=McCartan |first1=S. D. |title=Door Spaces Are Identifiable |journal=Proceedings of the Royal Irish Academy. Section A: Mathematical and Physical Sciences |date=1987 |volume=87A |issue=1 |pages=13–16 |jstor=20489255 |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/20489255 |issn=0035-8975}}</ref>  Such spaces are necessarily infinite.

There are exactly three types of connected door spaces <math>(X,\tau)</math>:{{sfn|McCartan|1987|loc=Corollary 3}}<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Wu |first1=Jianfeng |last2=Wang |first2=Chunli |last3=Zhang |first3=Dong |title=Connected door spaces and topological solutions of equations |journal=Aequationes Mathematicae |date=2018 |volume=92 |issue=6 |pages=1149–1161 |doi=10.1007/s00010-018-0577-0 |arxiv=1809.03085 |s2cid=253598359 |issn=0001-9054}} Theorem 1</ref>
* a space with the [[excluded point topology]];
* a space with the [[particular point topology|included point topology]];
* a space with topology <math>\tau</math> such that <math>\tau\setminus\{\emptyset\}</math> is a [[free ultrafilter]] on <math>X.</math>
